lesson.title: Fear on Trial: The Salem Witch Trials of 1692
lesson.summary: A wave of accusations in Salem Village during 1692 led to the deaths of about twenty people, exposing how deeply Puritan religious anxiety, social tension, and a shaky colonial government could combine into a devastating panic.
lesson.body:
In January 1692, two young girls in Salem Village, Massachusetts, nine year old Betty Parris and her eleven year old cousin Abigail Williams, began suffering strange fits: contorting their bodies, crying out, and complaining of being pinched or bitten by unseen forces. Betty was the daughter of the village's minister, Samuel Parris, and when a local doctor could find no physical explanation for the girls' behavior, he suggested the unthinkable but, to Puritans steeped in a worldview shaped by generations of religious teaching since the founding of Massachusetts Bay Colony, entirely plausible cause: witchcraft.

Pressured to name their tormentors, the girls accused three women who occupied vulnerable, marginal positions in Salem society: Tituba, an enslaved woman in the Parris household, along with Sarah Good and Sarah Osborne, both poor and already subject to local suspicion. Tituba, after harsh questioning, confessed to practicing witchcraft and offered vivid, elaborate testimony about other witches conspiring against the village, testimony that poured fuel on a fire already spreading. Over the following months accusations multiplied rapidly, eventually implicating well over a hundred people across Salem and neighboring communities, including some respected church members and even a former minister.

Governor William Phips, who had just arrived that same year under Massachusetts Bay's new royal charter following years of political instability after the colony's earlier charter was revoked, established a special Court of Oyer and Terminer to handle the flood of cases, with Chief Justice William Stoughton presiding. Controversially, the court allowed spectral evidence, testimony that a person's spirit or specter had appeared to and tormented a witness, even while the accused's physical body was demonstrably elsewhere. This evidentiary standard made denial nearly impossible to disprove and confession, paradoxically, one of the safest responses, since confessed witches were rarely executed while those who maintained their innocence often were.

Between June and September of 1692, nineteen people were hanged on Salem's Gallows Hill after being convicted, and one man, Giles Corey, was pressed to death under heavy stones after refusing to enter a plea at all. Several more accused people died in jail awaiting trial. As the accusations spread to increasingly prominent and clearly innocent members of society, skepticism grew, including from influential ministers like Increase Mather, who warned against convicting on such flimsy evidence. Phips dissolved the Court of Oyer and Terminer in October 1692, and a successor court that disallowed spectral evidence acquitted most remaining defendants, with Phips pardoning others by 1693. The episode left a lasting scar on Massachusetts Bay's identity and remains one of the most studied examples of how religious conviction, social pressure, and flawed legal procedure can combine into tragedy.
